lessons.title: Civilisation, cities and the Indus Valley

videos.title: Indus Valley Civilisation introduction (parent to choose)

warmup.front: In the Neolithic Age, where did many people live?
warmup.back: In small villages, practising agriculture and domesticating animals.

cards.title: From villages to cities
cards.body: With better methods of agriculture, surplus food was produced. So people could now devote more time to other activities. Gradually, villages grew into towns, and towns into cities; and the first great civilisations of the world were born.

cards.title: What is a civilisation?
cards.body: "Civilisation is said to occur when a society is in an advanced state of social development."

cards.title: City and urbanisation
cards.body: "A city is a large and densely populated area. Cities are also known as urban areas." "When more and more people start moving from villages to towns and cities, the process is called urbanisation."
cards.reveal: Urbanisation is one of the key features of civilisation.

cards.title: Life in a city
cards.body: In cities, people have occupations other than farming: traders, jewellery makers, writers and artists. Rulers and the ruling class usually live in cities.
cards.example: Public facilities: roads, a drainage system, public halls, and granaries.

cards.title: The Indus Valley Civilisation (IVC)
cards.body: About 4,700 years ago, the largest Bronze Age civilisation in the world emerged in the north-western part of the Indian subcontinent. It was born in the valley of the Indus River, so it is called the Indus Valley Civilisation (IVC). It is also known as the Harappan culture.
cards.didYouKnow: It was spread over about 650,000 sq. km, and more than 1,400 sites have been discovered to date.

cards.title: Important IVC sites
cards.body: Mohenjodaro and Harappa (in Pakistan), Dholavira and Lothal in Gujarat, Rakhigarhi and Banawali in Haryana, Ropar in Punjab, Kalibangan in Rajasthan, and Alamgirpur in Uttar Pradesh.
cards.reveal: It evolved from village communities between 7000 and 5000 BCE, and had many large urban centres between 2,600 and 1,900 BCE.

practice.explanation: This is the book’s definition of urbanisation (p.27).

keyRules: Civilisation is said to occur when a society is in an advanced state of social development.
A city is a large and densely populated area. Cities are also known as urban areas.
When more and more people start moving from villages to towns and cities, the process is called urbanisation.
Since this culture was born in the valley of the Indus River, it is popularly known as the Indus Valley Civilisation (IVC).

lessons.title: Town planning: citadel, Great Bath and drains

videos.title: Mohenjodaro town planning and Great Bath (parent to choose)

cards.title: Well-planned cities
cards.body: The most striking feature of the Indus Valley Civilisation was the well-planned nature of its cities. Mohenjodaro was a planned city with streets laid out in a grid pattern, that is, all the streets cut each other at right angles.

cards.title: The upper town (citadel)
cards.body: The upper town was built on a massive platform constructed of baked brick. Archaeologists call this area the citadel or acropolis. It might have been the administrative centre of the city.

cards.title: The lower town
cards.body: The lower town had the houses of the common people, with walls of baked bricks. The rooms were arranged around a courtyard. Each house had a single entrance, and one of every three houses had a well.
cards.didYouKnow: Many houses had a separate bathing area, and some were double-storeyed.

cards.title: The Great Bath
cards.body: Within the citadel at Mohenjodaro: a rectangular tank made of fired bricks closely fitted together, made waterproof by a thick layer of bitumen (tar).
cards.example: Rooms along its sides (one with a large well that supplied water), an outlet to a brick drain for dirty water, and flights of steps from opposite sides to the bottom.
cards.reveal: It might have been used for a bath before important functions and ceremonies.

cards.title: The granary and the drains
cards.body: To the west of the bath, a massive brick platform may have been a granary (a similar one was found at Harappa). Drains in houses led to a cesspool or manhole; drains along the main roads were covered and were inspected and cleaned regularly.

cards.title: Were there rulers?
cards.body: Straight roads, walled citadels and well-maintained drains mean there was a high standard of administration. But until the script of the IVC is deciphered, we cannot say much about the nature of government.

The drainage system of the Indus cities stands out as remarkable among the cities of the world at that time.

lessons.title: Food, clothes and the Indus script

videos.title: Indus Valley food, clothes and script (parent to choose)

cards.title: What did the people eat?
cards.body: Cereals like wheat and barley, pulses, oilseeds like mustard and sesame, and millets like bajra, ragi and jowar. Remains of these crops have been found from the excavated sites.
cards.example: Fish, meat, milk, date and fruit were also a part of the diet.
cards.reveal: We do not find much evidence of the cultivation of rice.

cards.title: What did they wear?
cards.body: Archaeologists have found evidence of cotton and woven cloth. Spindles made of clay have been found in many sites. (Spindles are used to spin cotton thread.)
cards.example: Men wore long, flowing cloth; the women may have worn skirts. Both seem to have draped a shawl over their shoulders.

cards.title: Ornaments
cards.body: Both men and women wore ornaments made of gold, silver, faience and beads of semi-precious stones like jade, lapis lazuli, cornelian and agate. Bangles, earrings and necklaces seem to have been popular.
cards.didYouKnow: The women applied kajal (kohl) on their eyes and painted their lips.

cards.title: Did they know how to write?
cards.body: Yes. They wrote in one of the world’s earliest known scripts. The script can be seen on seals made of baked clay and steatite (a soft stone that can be carved easily).
cards.reveal: The writing was mainly brief inscriptions, written from the right to the left. Historians are still trying to decipher the script.

practice.explanation: (Spindles are used to spin cotton thread.) Spindles made of clay were found in many sites (p.30).

lessons.title: Metals, pottery, art, seals and weights

videos.title: Indus Valley seals, dancing girl and crafts (parent to choose)

cards.title: Metallurgy
cards.body: The Indus people alloyed copper and tin to make bronze, which was stronger and more malleable than copper. Copper tools: razors, hooks, sickles, axes, nails and needles. Knives, axes and chisels were made of stone.
cards.reveal: There is no evidence for the use of iron to make objects, but iron minerals like hematite were used to make pigments.

cards.title: Pottery
cards.body: Besides agriculture, probably the most important occupation of the Indus people was pottery. Many pots were painted red, with designs in black suggesting geometric patterns.

cards.title: Art and Craft
cards.body: Two finely sculpted works of art from Mohenjodaro: the bust of a bearded man with his robe thrown over one shoulder, and the famed ‘dancing girl’ in bronze.
cards.example: Terracotta toys with moving parts: bulls and rams that could shake their heads and tails, and toy birds which could move up and down ropes.

cards.title: Seals
cards.body: Many seals were found, mainly made of steatite. Many show figures of animals, with writing on the top portion. Most are square in shape, a few round and some cylindrical.
cards.reveal: They were used for trade: pressed into soft clay to seal the mouths of jars and sacks of grain. Some were worn around the neck or arm, perhaps as a kind of identity card.

cards.title: Weights and Measures
cards.body: Cube-shaped stone weights in graduated sizes have been found. The smallest weight found is 0.856 grams and the most common weight is approximately 13.7 grams.
cards.didYouKnow: They seem to be uniform throughout the IVC, which must have made trade between the cities much easier.

lessons.title: Religion, trade and the decline of the IVC

videos.title: Indus Valley trade and decline (parent to choose)

cards.title: Religion
cards.body: Not much can be said with certainty. They may have worshipped a male yogic figure depicted in some of the seals. Archaeologists have named him ‘Pasupati’ and think the figure represents an early form of Shiva. They may also have worshipped mother goddesses and nature.
cards.reveal: Cemeteries at Harappa, Lothal and a few other sites show that the dead were buried wearing ornaments and with a few pots.

cards.title: Trade by land and by sea
cards.body: The IVC had a flourishing system of trade—both by land and by sea. Grains probably came from the villages around the cities, and the villages may have traded grain for goods produced in the cities. The Indus river system must have been used for trade.

cards.title: Trade with far-away lands
cards.body: Ornaments made in the Indus Valley have been found in Mesopotamia, which suggests trade between the two civilisations. A dockyard found at Lothal suggests overseas trade with western Asia.

cards.title: The decline
cards.body: This advanced civilisation appears to have declined suddenly after 2000 BCE. The exact causes of its decline remain a mystery, but a few reasons have been suggested.

cards.title: Suggested reasons
cards.body: Repeated natural and environmental disasters (earthquakes, floods or drought; rivers changing course, crops failing, epidemics); the falling quality of the soil and desertification due to excessive deforestation; the authority that kept the civilisation together losing control.
cards.reveal: Gradually, people would have moved away, and the cities would have crumbled.

questionBank.prompt: Which of the following correctly describe the Indus Valley Civilisation?
options: It was a Bronze age civilisation
questionBank.answer: It was a Bronze age civilisation
questionBank.explanation: About 4,700 years ago, the largest Bronze Age civilisation in the world emerged (p.28).

questionBank.prompt: Mention two places in Pakistan and two in India, where Indus Valley sites have been found.
questionBank.modelAnswer: Pakistan: Mohenjodaro and Harappa. India: for example, Dholavira and Lothal (Gujarat), Rakhigarhi and Banawali (Haryana), Ropar (Punjab), Kalibangan (Rajasthan), Alamgirpur (Uttar Pradesh).
questionBank.explanation: Any two Indian sites from p.28 are right.

questionBank.prompt: 'The Indus Valley civilisation had all the pre-conditions for it to be called a civilisation.' Do you agree? Justify your answer.
questionBank.modelAnswer: Yes. With better agriculture there was surplus food, so people could do other things. It had large planned cities (urbanisation), people with occupations other than farming, a script, art and craft, trade by land and sea, and a high standard of administration.
questionBank.explanation: Use what the chapter says makes a civilisation (p.27) and what the IVC had (pp.28–32).

questionBank.prompt: About how many years ago did the IVC emerge?
questionBank.explanation: About 4,700 years ago (p.28).

questionBank.prompt: More than ____ Indus Valley Civilisation sites have been discovered to date.
questionBank.explanation: More than 1,400 IVC sites have been discovered (p.28).

questionBank.prompt: Which of these is NOT something cities usually have, as the book lists it?
questionBank.explanation: Cities usually have roads, a drainage system, public halls, and granaries (p.27).

questionBank.prompt: Identify the structure: it was rectangular in shape; flights of steps from opposite sides led to its bottom; there were several rooms along the other two sides of it; there was a large well in one of the rooms.
questionBank.explanation: All four clues describe the Great Bath (p.29).

questionBank.prompt: The Indus Valley people built the walls of their houses with baked bricks. Which of the following statements correctly explains the reason behind it?
options: Baked bricks would prevent the houses from being washed away by floods.
Houses made of baked bricks could withstand attacks by enemies.
Houses made of baked bricks were strong and durable.
Houses made of baked bricks could protect people from volcanoes.
questionBank.answer: Houses made of baked bricks were strong and durable.
questionBank.explanation: The pages say the walls were made with baked bricks (p.28) but not why. Strong and durable is the general reason.

questionBank.prompt: The Indus people possibly gave importance to personal hygiene. Which features of town planning are evidence of that? (i) underground drainage (ii) a courtyard in each house (iii) separate bathing areas in many houses (iv) houses on raised platforms
questionBank.explanation: The careful drainage system and the separate bathing areas in many houses (p.29) are about keeping clean.

questionBank.prompt: What were the two parts into which the Indus Valley cities were divided?
questionBank.modelAnswer: The upper town (the citadel or acropolis) and the lower town.
questionBank.explanation: The city was divided into two parts—the upper town and the lower town (p.28).

questionBank.prompt: Mention any two features of the Great Bath that led archaeologists to identify it as a public bath.
questionBank.modelAnswer: It was a rectangular tank of fired bricks made waterproof with bitumen; there were rooms along its sides, one with a large well that supplied water; dirty water drained out to a brick drain; flights of steps from opposite sides led to the bottom.
questionBank.explanation: Any two of the four features on p.29.

questionBank.prompt: What was found to the west of the Great Bath?
options: A massive brick platform, perhaps a granary
questionBank.answer: A massive brick platform, perhaps a granary
questionBank.explanation: To the west of the bath, a massive brick platform has been excavated; it might have been a granary (p.29).

questionBank.prompt: Most of the houses in the lower town were plain and uniform in plan.
questionBank.explanation: "Most of the houses were plain and uniform in plan" (p.29).

questionBank.prompt: Which of the following artefacts is most associated with the writing system of the Indus Valley people?
questionBank.explanation: The script can be seen on seals found at the IVC sites (p.30).

questionBank.modelAnswer: Cereals like wheat and barley, pulses, oilseeds like mustard and sesame, and millets like bajra, ragi and jowar. Fish, meat, milk, date and fruit were also a part of the diet. There is not much evidence of rice.
questionBank.explanation: All of these are listed on pp.29–30.

questionBank.prompt: Describe the clothes and ornaments worn by the people of the IVC.
questionBank.modelAnswer: They wore cotton, woven cloth (spindles of clay were found). Men wore long, flowing cloth; women may have worn skirts; both draped a shawl over their shoulders. Men and women wore ornaments of gold, silver, faience and beads of jade, lapis lazuli, cornelian and agate; bangles, earrings and necklaces were popular. Women applied kajal and painted their lips.

questionBank.prompt: Which semi-precious stone is in the book’s list?
questionBank.explanation: Beads of semi-precious stones like jade, lapis lazuli, cornelian and agate (p.30).

questionBank.prompt: Fish, meat and milk were also a part of the diet of the Indus people.
questionBank.explanation: Fish, meat, milk, date and fruit were also a part of the diet (p.30).

questionBank.modelAnswer: The bust of a bearded man and the famed ‘dancing girl’ in bronze, from Mohenjodaro; terracotta toys with moving parts, like bulls and rams that could shake their heads and tails; pots painted red with black geometric designs.

questionBank.prompt: Assertion (A): The Indus Valley Civilisation suddenly came to an end after 2,000 BCE. Reason (R): There is strong evidence that frequent wars brought the Indus Valley Civilisation to an end.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questionBank.answer: A is true but R is false
questionBank.explanation: A is true: it declined suddenly after 2000 BCE. R is false: the exact causes remain a mystery, and wars are not among the suggested reasons (p.32).

questionBank.prompt: Examine the reasons for the decline of the IVC.
questionBank.modelAnswer: The exact causes remain a mystery. Suggested reasons: repeated natural and environmental disasters such as earthquakes, floods or drought (rivers changing course, crops failing, epidemics); the falling quality of the soil and desertification due to excessive deforestation; and the authority that kept the civilisation together losing control, so people moved away and the cities crumbled.
questionBank.explanation: All three reasons are on p.32.
